standard_text: Describe qualitatively the functional relationship between two quantities by analyzing a graph (e.g., where the function is increasing or decreasing, linear or nonlinear, has a maximum or minimum value). Sketch a graph that exhibits the qualitative features of a function that has been verbally described.

progression.narrative:
This standard runs in two mirror-image directions. First students must READ a graph qualitatively -- look at a curve and say, in words, what the relationship does: where it is increasing, decreasing, or constant; whether it is linear (a straight, constant rate) or nonlinear (a curve, a varying rate); and where it reaches a maximum or minimum. Then they must run the same logic backward and SKETCH a graph from a verbal description, turning words like 'rises quickly, levels off, then drops' into the correct sequence of rising, flat, and falling pieces. The one atom underneath both directions is the direction of change over an interval: as you move left to right, is the output going up, going down, or holding level? Everything else -- max/min, linear/nonlinear, faster/slower -- is built from that atom read across intervals.

So the arc begins by making sure students can orient to a graph (which axis is the input, read left to right) and name the direction of a single piece. From there they classify the whole graph's behavior with no context, then evaluate feature statements (max/min, linear/nonlinear, 'always increasing') for truth. Next the context arrives: match a real situation to its qualitative behavior, then analyze a graph in context by describing an interval and interpreting its highest or lowest point. The At-Proficiency capstone reverses the flow -- SKETCH a graph that matches a described situation, showing stops as flat segments and 'faster' as a steeper slope. The Above-Proficiency synthesis interprets intervals, extrema, and changing rates in context and draws conclusions. The through-line we keep naming: a graph is a story read left to right, and 'increasing/decreasing,' 'faster/slower,' and 'max/min' are the words that tell that story.

steps.rationale: The entry move: read a graph left to right and classify its overall behavior (increasing, decreasing, or a single turn) with no context. This settles the atom -- direction of change -- before context or multiple features are layered on.

Once a whole-graph shape can be named, students judge specific feature statements (has a maximum/minimum, linear vs nonlinear, 'always increasing') as true or false. This forces checking a claim against the WHOLE graph, not one convenient part.

Now the qualitative behavior lives inside a real-world story. Students translate a described situation into the correct ordered sequence of behaviors (increase, stay, decrease), the on-grade bridge from bare graphs to context.

The core analysis expectation: given a graph in context, describe what happens on a named interval and interpret what the highest or lowest point means in the situation. Combines interval-direction with max/min meaning.

The At-Proficiency capstone reverses the flow: construct a graph that matches a verbal description, translating 'stops' into flat segments and 'faster' into steeper slopes. Producing a graph, not just reading one, is the standard's second explicit demand.

The Above-Proficiency synthesis: interpret intervals, extrema, and CHANGING RATES (faster/slower) of a graph in context and draw conclusions -- proving students read steepness as rate, not height, and can reason across a multi-feature graph.

skills.name: Read a coordinate graph's axes and locate points left to right

prerequisite_skill.description: Read a coordinate graph: know the horizontal axis is the input and the vertical axis is the output, locate a point, and read the graph from left to right.
prerequisite_skill.check_question: On a graph of distance over time, which axis shows time, and which direction do you read the graph?

skills.i_do_script: Before I can describe a graph I have to know how to read it. The bottom (horizontal) axis is the INPUT -- often time -- and the side (vertical) axis is the OUTPUT -- like distance or height. Watch: on a distance-vs-time graph, a point at 3 across and 8 up means 'at time 3, distance is 8.' And I always read a graph left to right, like reading a sentence -- the left side is the beginning of the story, the right side is the end.

canonical_error.pattern: Swaps the axes -- treats the vertical (output) quantity as the input, or reads the graph right to left
canonical_error.example: On a distance-vs-time graph, reads a point as 'at distance 3, time is 8' instead of 'at time 3, distance is 8'
canonical_error.why: The student does not hold the convention that the horizontal axis is the input read left to right. Swapping the axes (or the reading direction) reverses every later judgment about what comes first and whether the graph is 'increasing.'

skills.item_template: A described coordinate graph with labeled axes and one point. Student names which axis is the input and reads the point in (input, output) order. Short response fluency bank.

sample_items.stem: On a graph of temperature over time, which axis shows time?
sample_items.answer: The horizontal (bottom) axis.

sample_items.stem: A point on a distance-vs-time graph is 4 across and 10 up. Read it as 'at time ___, distance is ___.'
sample_items.answer: At time 4, distance is 10.

sample_items.stem: Which side of a graph shows the beginning of the story?
sample_items.answer: The left side (you read left to right).

sample_items.stem: On a height-vs-time graph, is height shown on the horizontal axis or the vertical axis?
sample_items.answer: The vertical (side) axis.

redirect_script.stop: Which axis is the input -- across or up?
redirect_script.prompt: Point to the bottom axis and say 'input' (usually time); point to the side axis and say 'output.' Read the point as (across, up) and read the whole graph left to right, like a sentence.
redirect_script.praise: You read across first, then up, and started at the left -- that's how a graph tells its story.

vocabulary.definition: The bottom axis of a graph; it shows the input quantity, often time.
The side axis of a graph; it shows the output quantity that depends on the input.
A stretch of the input axis between two points, like 'from time 2 to time 5.'

worked_example_script.text: Sketch labeled axes: 'Time' across the bottom, 'Height' up the side. Mark a point at 2 across, 6 up.
Which axis is the input? What does the point say in (time, height) order?
Time is the bottom axis. The point is at time 2, height 6 -- 2 across, then 6 up.
If a student says 'height 2, time 6,' ask 'which axis do we read first -- the across one or the up one?'
Your turn: on a distance-vs-time graph, read the point at 5 across and 3 up.

skills.name: Name whether a piece of a graph is increasing, decreasing, or constant

prerequisite_skill.description: Read a single piece of a graph left to right and say whether the output goes up (increasing), down (decreasing), or stays level (constant).
prerequisite_skill.check_question: As you move left to right, a line goes from low up to high. Is it increasing or decreasing?

skills.i_do_script: The whole standard rests on one move: reading a piece of a graph left to right and naming its direction. If the line goes UP as I move right, it is INCREASING. If it goes DOWN as I move right, it is DECREASING. If it stays level (flat), it is CONSTANT. Watch: a line that starts at 8 on the left and slides down to 2 on the right is DECREASING -- even though the numbers are big, the direction is downhill. It is the direction of travel that matters, not how high up the line sits.

canonical_error.pattern: Judges increasing/decreasing by how HIGH the values are (or that they are positive) instead of by the direction the line travels left to right
canonical_error.example: Calls a line that falls from 8 down to 2 'increasing' because the values are large/high, instead of 'decreasing'
canonical_error.why: The student confuses the height/position of the graph with its direction of change. 'Increasing' means the output GOES UP as the input increases -- an uphill line -- regardless of whether the values themselves are large or small.

skills.item_template: A described single graph segment. Student names increasing, decreasing, or constant. Short response fluency bank.

sample_items.stem: As you read left to right, a line rises from low to high. Increasing, decreasing, or constant?
sample_items.answer: Increasing

sample_items.stem: A line falls from 9 on the left down to 1 on the right. Increasing, decreasing, or constant?
sample_items.answer: Decreasing

sample_items.stem: A line stays flat at a height of 5 the whole way across. Increasing, decreasing, or constant?
sample_items.answer: Constant

sample_items.stem: A line sits high the whole way but slopes gently downhill as you move right. Is it increasing or decreasing?
sample_items.answer: Decreasing (it goes down as you move right, even though it stays high).

redirect_script.stop: Which way does the line travel as you move right?
redirect_script.prompt: Put your finger on the left end and trace to the right. If your finger goes up, it's increasing; down, decreasing; level, constant. Ignore how high the line sits -- watch the direction.
redirect_script.praise: You read the direction of travel, not the height -- that's exactly what increasing and decreasing mean.

vocabulary.definition: The output goes up as you move left to right (an uphill line).
The output goes down as you move left to right (a downhill line).
The output holds level -- it does not change as the input increases (a flat line).

worked_example_script.text: Describe a line that starts at 7 on the left and drops steadily to 2 on the right.
Trace left to right -- does your finger go up or down?
Down. So the function is DECREASING, even though it starts high. Direction beats height.
If a student says 'increasing because the numbers are big,' ask 'but which way does the line GO as we move right?'
Your turn: a line rises from 1 up to 6 across the graph -- increasing or decreasing?

skills.name: Match a graph to the qualitative description of its overall behavior
skills.i_do_script: To match a graph to a description, I trace it left to right and narrate its direction, noticing any TURN. Watch a graph that climbs to a peak in the middle and then falls: left to right it goes up, then down, so it 'increases then decreases.' The trap is reading the shape backward -- a hill (up then down) is NOT the same as a valley (down then up). I always start at the left end and say the directions in the order they happen.

canonical_error.pattern: Reads the turn backward -- calls an 'increases then decreases' graph 'decreases then increases' (or reads the graph right to left)
canonical_error.example: For a graph shaped like a hill (rises to a peak, then falls), picks 'decreases then increases' instead of 'increases then decreases'
canonical_error.why: The student either reads the graph right to left or fixes on the ending direction and reverses the order of the two behaviors. A hill and a valley are opposite shapes; the order must be read left to right.

skills.item_template: A verbally described graph (no context). Student selects the matching behavior description. MC.

sample_items.stem: A graph starts low on the left and rises steadily all the way to the right. Which description fits?
sample_items.answer: The function is always increasing.
sample_items.distractor_logic: Left to right it only goes up. The 'turn' options add a direction change that isn't there.

sample_items.stem: Reading left to right, a graph climbs to a peak in the middle, then falls. Which description fits?
sample_items.answer: The function increases then decreases.
sample_items.distractor_logic: A hill goes up then down. 'Decreases then increases' reads the turn backward.

sample_items.stem: Reading left to right, a graph drops to a low point in the middle, then climbs back up. Which description fits?
sample_items.answer: The function decreases then increases.
sample_items.distractor_logic: A valley goes down then up; 'increases then decreases' is the reversed (hill) reading.

sample_items.stem: A graph falls steadily from the upper left to the lower right. Which description fits?
sample_items.answer: The function is always decreasing.
sample_items.distractor_logic: Downhill the whole way is always decreasing; the high starting point tempts an 'increasing' misread.

redirect_script.stop: Start at the LEFT -- which way first?
redirect_script.prompt: Put your finger on the left end and trace right. Say each direction in order: up first or down first? A hill is 'up then down'; a valley is 'down then up.' Match the order you traced.
redirect_script.praise: You read the directions left to right in order -- that's how you tell a hill from a valley.

vocabulary.definition: A description of a graph in words (up, down, flat, a turn) rather than exact numbers.
A graph that rises to a high point and then falls -- a hill shape with a maximum.

worked_example_script.text: Describe a graph that dips to a low point in the middle, then rises to the right.
Trace left to right -- which direction first, and which second?
Down first, then up. So it 'decreases then increases' -- a valley shape.
If a student says 'increases then decreases,' ask 'did the graph go UP first or DOWN first as we moved right?'
Your turn: a graph rises to a peak, then falls. Which description?

practice_problems.stem: A line goes uphill the whole way, left to right. Increasing or decreasing?
practice_problems.answer: Increasing.

practice_problems.stem: What shape is 'increases then decreases' -- a hill or a valley?
practice_problems.answer: A hill (up to a peak, then down).

practice_problems.stem: A graph climbs to a peak in the middle, then falls. Which description fits: always increasing, always decreasing, increases then decreases, or decreases then increases?
practice_problems.answer: Increases then decreases.
practice_problems.notes: Baits reading the turn backward.

practice_problems.stem: A graph drops to a low point, then rises. Which description fits?
practice_problems.answer: Decreases then increases.
practice_problems.notes: Valley shape; the reversed reading gives a hill.

practice_problems.stem: Maya matched a graph to a description. Find and fix her mistake.
shown_work: The graph rises to a peak in the middle, then falls back down.
practice_problems.answer: Maya read the turn backward. Traced left to right, the graph goes UP first (to the peak) and DOWN second, so it 'increases then decreases' -- a hill, not a valley.
practice_problems.notes: Canonical error: reversed turn order.

practice_problems.stem: A graph falls steadily from upper left to lower right with no turn. Which description fits?
practice_problems.answer: Always decreasing.
practice_problems.notes: High start tempts an 'increasing' misread.

practice_problems.stem: Sketch-in-words: describe a graph that would match 'decreases then increases,' and name the special point at the turn.
practice_problems.answer: A downhill line to a lowest point in the middle, then an uphill line -- a valley. The turn is a minimum.
practice_problems.notes: Reverse direction: produce a matching shape and name the extremum.

practice_problems.stem: Two graphs: Graph A goes up then down; Graph B goes up the whole way. Which one has a maximum in the middle, and why?
practice_problems.answer: Graph A -- it rises to a peak and then falls, so the peak is a maximum. Graph B keeps rising, so its highest value is at the far right end, not a turning-point maximum in the middle.
practice_problems.notes: Connects turn shape to where a maximum lives.

activities.title: Hill, Valley, or Straight?
materials: Card set: 12 word-descriptions of graphs (some always up/down, some hills, some valleys)
activities.instructions:
1. Sort each description card into 'Always Increasing,' 'Always Decreasing,' 'Increases then Decreases (hill),' or 'Decreases then Increases (valley).'
2. For each hill and valley card, mark where the maximum or minimum would be.
3. Trade piles with another group and check each other's sorts.
4. Debrief: how do you tell a hill from a valley just from the word order?

cards.text: climbs to a peak, then drops
dips to a low point, then climbs
up to a maximum, then back down
down to a minimum, then back up

activities.title: Which Way First?
activities.instructions:
1. Read Maya's claim that a hill-shaped graph 'decreases then increases.'
2. Trace the graph left to right and write the two directions in the order they happen.
3. Decide whether it is a hill or a valley and fix the description.
4. Write a rule for telling the order of behaviors.

content.worked_problem: A graph rises to a peak, then falls. Maya wrote 'decreases then increases.'
content.error_step: Maya read the turn backward (or read right to left).
content.why: Left to right the graph goes UP first, then DOWN, so it 'increases then decreases.'

strategy_links.why: The reversed-turn read is a precise, nameable error that a find-and-fix targeting the left-to-right order exposes cleanly.
Thinking aloud 'up first, then down' while tracing models the ordered left-to-right read.
Think-pair-share on 'is this a hill or a valley?' surfaces the turn-order confusion for discussion.

questioning_prompts: Which direction does the graph go first, left to right?
Is this a hill or a valley?
Where is the turning point, and is it a peak or a low point?
Did you read the graph left to right?
Does your description name the behaviors in the order they happen?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student calls a hill-shaped graph 'decreases then increases' (reads the turn backward).
misconception_redirects.say: Put your finger on the left end and trace right. Say each direction in order: up first or down first? A hill is 'up then down'; a valley is 'down then up.' Match the order you traced.
misconception_redirects.praise: You read the directions left to right in order -- that's how you tell a hill from a valley.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student calls a downhill line 'increasing' because it starts high.
misconception_redirects.say: Watch the direction of travel, not the starting height. Trace left to right -- if your finger goes down, it's decreasing, even from a high start.
misconception_redirects.praise: You judged by the direction of travel, not the height -- that's the real meaning of decreasing.

quick_checks.prompt: A graph rises to a peak, then falls. Which description fits?
quick_checks.look_for: 'Increases then decreases.' A 'decreases then increases' answer means the turn was read backward.

quick_checks.prompt: A graph goes downhill the whole way. Which description fits?
quick_checks.look_for: 'Always decreasing.' An 'increasing' answer means the student is judging by height, not direction.

sentence_starters: Reading left to right, the graph goes ___ first, then ___.
This is a ___ (hill/valley), so the function ___ then ___.

worked_solution.stem: Reading left to right, a graph rises to a high point in the middle and then falls. Which description fits, and what is the turning point called?
worked_solution.answer: It increases then decreases; the turning point is a maximum.

steps.math: start at the left end and trace right
steps.annotation: Always read a graph left to right, like a sentence.

steps.math: up to the peak, then down after it
steps.annotation: Name the two directions in the order they happen.
Up-then-down is a hill, not a valley.
The highest point where it turns is the maximum value.

faded_example.stem: Reading left to right, a graph drops to a low point in the middle and then rises. Which description fits, and what is the turning point called?
faded_example.answer: It decreases then increases; the turning point is a minimum.

steps.math: trace the graph left to right
steps.annotation: Read the story from the left end.

steps.math: down to the low point first
steps.annotation: Name the first direction.
Name the second direction (after the low point) and give the full description.
State whether the turning point is a maximum or a minimum.

skills.name: Evaluate whether statements about a graph's features are true
skills.i_do_script: Now I test specific claims about a graph -- about its maximum or minimum, whether it is linear or nonlinear, and whether it is 'always' increasing or decreasing. The key move is to check each claim against the WHOLE graph, not just one part. Watch a graph that rises then falls: 'the function is always increasing' is FALSE, because it only increases at the start; 'the function has a maximum' is TRUE, because the peak is a highest point. A word like 'always' has to hold everywhere.

canonical_error.pattern: Accepts a statement that is true for only PART of the graph as true for the whole (or swaps maximum and minimum, or calls a curved graph linear)
canonical_error.example: For a graph that rises then falls, marks 'the function is always increasing' TRUE because it increases at the start
canonical_error.why: The student checks one convenient piece and stops. Words like 'always' and features like a maximum must be tested against every part of the graph; a claim true on one interval can be false overall.

skills.item_template: A verbally described multi-feature graph (no context). Student selects the TRUE statement. MC.

sample_items.stem: A graph rises to a high point in the middle, then falls. Which statement is TRUE?
sample_items.answer: The function has a maximum value.
choices: The function has a maximum value.
The function has a minimum in the middle.
sample_items.distractor_logic: The peak is a maximum. 'Always increasing/decreasing' fails after/before the turn; the middle is a max, not a min.

sample_items.stem: A graph falls to a low point, then rises. Which statement is TRUE?
sample_items.answer: The function has a minimum value.
choices: The function has a minimum value.
The function has a maximum in the middle.
sample_items.distractor_logic: The low point is a minimum. The 'always' claims fail at the turn; the middle is a min, not a max.

sample_items.stem: A graph rises steadily, then becomes a flat horizontal segment for the rest. Which statement is TRUE?
sample_items.answer: The function increases, then stays constant.
choices: The function increases, then stays constant.
The function decreases at the end.
The function is nonlinear at the start.
sample_items.distractor_logic: It stops increasing when it goes flat, so 'always increasing' is false; it never decreases; a steady rise is linear, not nonlinear.

sample_items.stem: A graph goes up in a straight line, then curves upward more and more steeply. Which statement is TRUE?
sample_items.answer: The function is nonlinear overall.
choices: The function has a maximum in the middle.
sample_items.distractor_logic: A curving (varying-rate) part makes the whole graph nonlinear; it never decreases and has no middle peak.

redirect_script.stop: Does that hold for the WHOLE graph?
redirect_script.prompt: Test the claim on every part. Cover the graph with your hand and reveal it piece by piece: does 'always increasing' stay true after the turn? A word like 'always' has to work everywhere, not just at the start.
redirect_script.praise: You checked the claim across the whole graph, not just one part -- that's how you judge 'always' and max/min.

vocabulary.definition: The highest output the graph reaches -- the top of a peak.
The lowest output the graph reaches -- the bottom of a valley.
A straight-line graph with a constant rate of change.
A graph that curves (or bends) because the rate of change varies.

worked_example_script.text: Describe a graph that falls to a low point in the middle, then rises. List claims: 'always decreasing'; 'has a minimum'; 'has a maximum in the middle.'
Test each claim against the whole graph -- which one holds everywhere it needs to?
'Always decreasing' is false (it rises after the low point). 'Has a minimum' is true -- the low point. 'Maximum in the middle' is false; that low point is a minimum.
If a student marks 'always decreasing' true, ask 'what happens AFTER the low point -- does it still go down?'
Your turn: a graph rises then goes flat. Is 'always increasing' true or false?

practice_problems.stem: The highest point a graph reaches is called its ___.
practice_problems.answer: Maximum (value).

practice_problems.stem: A straight-line graph with a steady rate is called ___; a curved one is called ___.
practice_problems.answer: Linear; non-linear.

practice_problems.stem: A graph rises to a peak, then falls. True or false: 'The function is always increasing.'
practice_problems.answer: False -- it only increases up to the peak, then it decreases.
practice_problems.notes: Baits accepting a part-true claim as whole-true.

practice_problems.stem: A graph rises steadily, then goes flat. True or false: 'The function has a constant part.'
practice_problems.answer: True -- the flat segment is constant (no change).
practice_problems.notes: Constant = flat.

practice_problems.stem: Devon judged a statement about a graph. Find and fix the mistake.
shown_work: The graph rises to a high point in the middle, then falls back down.
Devon wrote: 'TRUE -- the function is always increasing.'
practice_problems.answer: It is only increasing up to the peak; after the peak it decreases, so 'always increasing' is FALSE. What IS true is that the graph has a maximum at the peak. Devon judged from the first part only.
practice_problems.notes: Canonical error: part-true accepted as whole-true.

practice_problems.stem: A graph goes up in a straight line, then curves and rises faster and faster. True or false: 'The whole graph is linear.'
practice_problems.answer: False -- the curving part has a varying rate, so the graph is non-linear overall.
practice_problems.notes: One curved part makes the whole nonlinear.

practice_problems.stem: Write one TRUE and one FALSE statement about a graph that falls to a low point and then rises. Explain each.
practice_problems.answer: True: 'the function has a minimum' (the low point). False: 'the function is always decreasing' (it rises after the low point).
practice_problems.notes: Produce-your-own true/false with justification.

practice_problems.stem: A classmate says 'the graph has a maximum' about a line that rises the whole way with no turn. Is that the same kind of maximum as a hill's peak? Explain.
practice_problems.answer: Its highest value is just the far-right endpoint, not a turning-point peak. A hill has a maximum in the MIDDLE where it turns from up to down; a steadily rising line only 'peaks' at its end.
practice_problems.notes: Distinguishes an endpoint high from a turning-point maximum.

1. Match each graph description to the ONE statement that is true for the whole graph.
2. Two statement cards are 'always' traps -- true for only part of a graph. Set them aside and explain the trap.

activities.title: Does 'Always' Hold?
activities.instructions:
1. Read Devon's claim that a hill-shaped graph is 'always increasing.'
2. Reveal the graph in two parts (before and after the peak) and test the claim on each part.
3. Rewrite a statement that IS true for the whole graph.
4. Write the rule for testing an 'always' claim.

content.worked_problem: A graph rises to a peak, then falls. Devon marked 'always increasing' TRUE.
content.error_step: Devon checked only the part before the peak.
content.why: After the peak the graph decreases, so 'always increasing' is false; the true feature is a maximum at the peak.

strategy_links.why: The part-true-as-whole-true error is precise; find-and-fix that tests the claim on every interval builds the checking habit.
Comparing a claim that holds everywhere to one that holds only at the start makes the 'always' criterion explicit.
A number-talk style 'true or false, defend it' routine surfaces max/min and linear/nonlinear reasoning out loud.

questioning_prompts: Does that claim hold for the WHOLE graph or just part of it?
Where is the maximum, and where is the minimum?
Is the graph straight (linear) or curved (nonlinear)?
What happens AFTER the turn?
Which word in the statement -- 'always,' 'maximum,' 'linear' -- do you need to test?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student marks an 'always increasing' claim true because the graph increases at the start.
misconception_redirects.say: Test the claim on every part. Cover the graph with your hand and reveal it piece by piece: does 'always increasing' stay true after the turn? A word like 'always' has to work everywhere, not just at the start.
misconception_redirects.praise: You checked the claim across the whole graph, not just one part -- that's how you judge 'always' and max/min.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student swaps maximum and minimum (calls a valley's low point a maximum).
misconception_redirects.say: A maximum is a high peak; a minimum is a low valley. Point to the highest and lowest spots and label them before you judge the statement.
misconception_redirects.praise: You matched the peak to maximum and the valley to minimum -- that's the right vocabulary.

quick_checks.prompt: A graph rises to a peak then falls. True or false: 'always increasing.'
quick_checks.look_for: False. A 'true' answer means the student checked only the first part.

quick_checks.prompt: A graph curves upward faster and faster. True or false: 'the graph is linear.'
quick_checks.look_for: False -- it is nonlinear. A 'true' answer means the student ignored the curve (varying rate).

sentence_starters: The claim is ___ because on the ___ part the graph ___.
The graph has a ___ (maximum/minimum) at the ___, so the true statement is ___.

worked_solution.stem: A graph falls to a low point in the middle, then rises. Decide which is true: (a) always decreasing; (b) has a minimum; (c) has a maximum in the middle.

steps.math: (a) test 'always decreasing' on the whole graph
steps.annotation: After the low point the graph rises, so it is NOT always decreasing -> FALSE.

steps.math: (b) the low point is the smallest output
steps.annotation: A lowest turning point is a minimum -> TRUE.

steps.math: (c) the middle point is the LOWEST, not highest
steps.annotation: That is a minimum, not a maximum -> FALSE.

steps.math: true statement: the function has a minimum
steps.annotation: Only the claim that holds for the whole graph survives.
